paras: The threatened lynching of Arthur Neill took place at Vinegar Bend, Washington County, Alabama, on August 22, 1910, when citizens talked of lynching a Black prisoner reported to have confessed to assaulting a white woman, Mrs. J. O. Gibson of Axis. Mobile deputies took him by freight train to the Mobile jail, and he was not harmed. Within weeks, reports said a second confession of his was false and that a grand jury had declined to hold him because he was "crazy" and had confessed though innocent.

On July 31, Mrs. Gibson was said to have been assaulted at Axis in Mobile County, and a Black man, Jesse Brown, was killed the same night. Another Black man, Bill Walker, also called Gus Walker, was arrested in Mississippi for the crime, and Mrs. Gibson picked him out at the Mobile jail as her assailant. Neill had been arrested in the same period and sentenced to ninety days for vagrancy at the Vinegar Bend stockade, owned by the Vinegar Bend Lumber Company.

According to the Mobile reports, blood was found on Neill's clothing when he was ordered to change into stripes on Sunday, August 21, and he then confessed to Warden Miller. The Montgomery Advertiser called it a "free and full confession," while the Birmingham Age-Herald said he "could not explain" the blood "and was forced to confess." Deputy Sheriff Wade and two other deputies came from Mobile the next morning, and Neill repeated the statement to them.

When word of the confession spread, there was "great excitement in the village" and "strong talk of a lynching." The Advertiser credited N. E. Turner, president of the lumber company, with calming the "irate citizens," and said he and the officers judged the stockade too weak to resist a mob. The deputies' version, given in the Age-Herald, was that they saw a mob forming and had the agent flag a fast freight train. Neill reached Mobile at about 6:25 p.m. and was taken to the jail "without undue excitement," although the Age-Herald's correspondent warned of excitement there that "may become serious later tonight."

On August 24, Neill, now named as Arthur McNeill, alias Neill, told Jailer Wade that he had also assaulted a white woman named Alice Davis near Pine Hill six years earlier. Her father, Amos Davis, said she had been dead for eight years, and people who knew McNeill said he often told stories that proved false. A special grand jury met in Mobile on August 31 to hear the cases of Walker and McNeill.

Walker's request to move his trial out of Mobile County was refused, and on September 8 he was sentenced to death for the murder of Jesse Brown, after which the assault cases were dropped. The same dispatch reported that the grand jury had not held McNeill because he was "crazy" and had been questioned by officers until he "weakened and confessed though innocent." No report of arrests among the Vinegar Bend crowd, or of what became of McNeill afterward, appears in the coverage.

The episode ran as Mobile specials in two Alabama dailies, the Montgomery Advertiser and the Birmingham Age-Herald, on August 23. The Age-Herald headlined that Neill "ADMITS HE IS THE ASSAILANT OF MRS. GIBSON" and "IS RUSHED TO THE MOBILE JAIL TO AVOID A LYNCHING," calling the crowd a "lynching bee," while the Advertiser's "NEGRO MAKES CONFESSION" described the confession as "alleged." Neither paper commented on the mob, and the Age-Herald still called him the "confessed assailant" on August 25.

The Age-Herald followed with "NEGRO'S STORY IS PROVEN FALSE" on August 26 and, on September 9, a brief report that he had confessed though innocent, placed beneath news of Walker's death sentence. No coverage of the episode in the Black press was found.

Accounts of Neill's guilt conflict: the August reports presented his confession as fact, Mrs. Gibson had earlier identified Walker, and the September 9 report, citing no named source, said the confession was false.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Arthur Neill
bases: A crowd at Vinegar Bend talked of lynching a Black prisoner after his reported confession, and officers moved him to Mobile to prevent mob violence; no one was harmed (A2, A3).

Neill was not killed: the papers report only 'strong talk of a lynching' and a mob forming, and he reached the Mobile jail 'without undue excitement' (A2, A3). The episode is a threatened lynching over an alleged assault on a white woman.

Two Mobile specials in different papers agree on the reported confession, the lynching talk at Vinegar Bend and the transfer by freight to Mobile (A2, A3), though they may share a Mobile correspondent.

framing.detail: The Age-Herald headlined 'ADMITS HE IS THE ASSAILANT OF MRS. GIBSON—IS RUSHED TO THE MOBILE JAIL TO AVOID A LYNCHING' and called the crowd a 'lynching bee', presenting the confession as fact without comment on the mob.
The Advertiser's 'NEGRO MAKES CONFESSION' story hedged the confession as 'alleged' and stressed the calming of 'irate citizens' by the company president.
Follow-ups headlined 'NEGRO'S STORY IS PROVEN FALSE' and later reported he confessed 'though innocent', while the Age-Herald still called him the 'confessed assailant' on Aug. 25.

info: Confession reported on Sunday, Aug. 21, 1910; lynching talk and transfer to Mobile on Aug. 22.
Vinegar Bend lumber-company stockade, Vinegar Bend, Washington County; prisoner moved to the Mobile County jail.
Arthur Neill, also called Arthur McNeill, alias Neill, described as 'a negro' serving a vagrancy sentence; no one was injured.
Alleged confession to assaulting Mrs. J. O. Gibson at Axis on July 31, and in one account to cutting her and her young brother; a later report says he was 'crazy' and confessed though innocent.
Citizens of Vinegar Bend; a 'mob forming' according to the deputies.
Neill was not lynched and was not held by the grand jury; his later disposition is not reported.
